newsitem.title: USA: Sex offender registry law an issue in upcoming trial.
newsitem.headline: Sex offender registry law an issue in upcoming trial.

text.p: - A highly public campaign to enact a law requiring sex offenders to register with authorities has become an issue in the trial of the man accused of killing the victim who inspired it.

Jury selection begins Monday in the rape-murder trial of Jesse Timmendequas, 34, a twice-convicted sex offender who was living in Hamilton Township with his past unknown to his neighbours. In July 1994, prosecutors say, he lured 7-year-old Megan Kanka into his home, raped her and strangled her.
The girl's body was found in a park two miles (3 km) away after a two-day search.

The incident prompted a highly public campaign to change the law in New Jersey -- and other states afterward -- led by the little girl's parents, Maureen and Richard Kanka. During that campaign, Timmendequas' criminal record was widely discussed.
That fact is the basis of a defence request that potential jurors be questioned about their knowledge of Megan's Law.
It requires sex offenders to register with police and empowers prosecutors to screen them for risk to the public -- with the public being told about those assessed as posing the highest risk.

Timmendequas' defence team asked that the trial be moved from Mercer County because of pretrial publicity. The judge decided instead to pick a jury from neighbouring Hunterdon County. That's the process that starts Monday and may take months to complete.
When the trial begins, the jurors will be bused the 20 miles (32 km) between Flemington and Trenton.
Megan's Law currently is in legal limbo. A series of rulings empower the state to require offenders to register and to consider offender appeals, but not to notify the public.
